questions.prompt: Which king united England and Denmark in the 11th century?
questions.fact: The story of him commanding the tide was staged to prove the opposite of what it is usually quoted for: that kings are powerless.

questions.prompt: The Antikythera mechanism was used to predict what?
questions.fact: Nothing of comparable gearing complexity appears again for well over a thousand years.

questions.prompt: Which country was ruled by the Tokugawa shogunate?
questions.fact: It closed the country to almost all foreign contact for over two centuries, permitting one Dutch trading post.

questions.prompt: Which US general accepted the Confederate surrender at Appomattox?
questions.fact: He let the defeated soldiers keep their horses, reasoning they would need them for spring planting.

questions.prompt: Which ancient wonder stood on the island of Pharos?
questions.fact: It stood for around 1,600 years before earthquakes finally brought it down, outlasting every other wonder but the pyramids.

questions.prompt: The Meiji Restoration ended rule by which class?
questions.fact: Samurai were compensated with government bonds, and many promptly lost everything investing them badly.

questions.prompt: Which European power colonised Brazil?
questions.fact: For a period in the 1800s the Portuguese court actually governed its empire from Rio rather than Lisbon.

questions.prompt: Which battle in 1066 preceded the Battle of Hastings by weeks?
questions.fact: Harold marched his army about 300 kilometres between the two battles, which is a plausible reason he lost the second.

questions.prompt: Which civilisation produced the Code of Hammurabi?
questions.fact: It set penalties by social rank, so the same offence cost a noble and a commoner very different amounts.

questions.prompt: Who was the first European monarch to break with the Roman Catholic Church in the 1530s?
questions.fact: The Pope had earlier given him a title defending the faith, which English monarchs still carry today.

questions.prompt: The Long March was a retreat by forces of which movement?
questions.fact: Roughly one in ten who set out arrived, but the survivors formed the leadership for the next forty years.

questions.prompt: Which empire was defeated at the Battle of Lepanto in 1571?
questions.fact: It was among the last great battles fought with oared galleys, a technology already being replaced by sail.

questions.prompt: Which treaty divided the New World between Spain and Portugal?
questions.fact: The line was drawn before anyone knew what was there, which is the accident that made Brazil Portuguese.

questions.prompt: Which city was destroyed by an earthquake and tsunami in 1755, shaking European thought?
questions.fact: It struck on a religious holiday with churches full, which prompted a wave of philosophical argument about divine justice.

questions.prompt: The Zulu kingdom rose to power in which region?
questions.fact: Its army defeated a British force at Isandlwana in 1879, one of the worst defeats a colonial army suffered in Africa.

questions.prompt: Which US document was adopted on 4 July 1776?
questions.fact: Most signatures were added weeks later, so the famous scene of everyone signing that day never happened.

questions.prompt: Which empire did Justinian I rule?
questions.fact: His legal code was rediscovered in medieval Italy and became the foundation of law across much of continental Europe.

questions.prompt: Which conflict was triggered by the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand?
questions.fact: The assassin got his chance only because the archduke's driver took a wrong turn and stopped to reverse.

questions.prompt: Which ancient people built Great Zimbabwe?
questions.fact: Colonial authorities spent decades insisting it must have been built by outsiders, against the archaeological evidence.

questions.prompt: The Suez Crisis of 1956 involved the nationalisation of what?
questions.fact: It ended when the United States pressured its own allies to withdraw, a moment often read as the end of British imperial reach.

questions.prompt: Which dynasty ruled China immediately before the Qing?
questions.fact: Its last emperor hanged himself on a hill overlooking the Forbidden City as rebels entered Beijing.

questions.prompt: Who led the Mongol invasion that sacked Baghdad in 1258?
questions.fact: The city's libraries were destroyed, and accounts describe the Tigris running black with ink from the books.

questions.prompt: Which country did Simón Bolívar first liberate from Spanish rule?
questions.fact: He declared independence three separate times before it held, losing and regaining the country in between.

questions.prompt: The Rosetta Stone was discovered during whose military campaign?
questions.fact: The expedition brought scholars as well as soldiers, and their survey created the modern study of ancient Egypt.

questions.prompt: Which country was partitioned in 1947 into two independent states?
questions.fact: The border was drawn in five weeks by a lawyer who had never previously visited the subcontinent.

questions.prompt: Which Viking is traditionally said to have reached North America around 1000?
questions.fact: A Norse settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland confirms Europeans arrived roughly 500 years before Columbus.

questions.prompt: The Reign of Terror occurred during which revolution?
questions.fact: Its chief architect was executed by the same method he had used on others, within a year of taking power.

questions.prompt: Which empire's capital was Persepolis?
questions.fact: Alexander burned it in 330 BC, an act his own officers reportedly tried to talk him out of.

questions.prompt: Who was the first person to be elected US president four times?
questions.fact: A constitutional amendment passed shortly after his death capped future presidents at two terms.

questions.prompt: Which country's revolution of 1979 replaced a monarchy with an Islamic republic?
questions.fact: The Shah left on what was officially described as a holiday, and never returned.

questions.prompt: The Elgin Marbles were removed from which building?
questions.fact: Their ownership has been formally disputed since Greek independence in the 1830s and remains unresolved.

questions.prompt: Which war ended with the Treaty of Ghent in 1814?
questions.fact: The largest battle of the war was fought after the treaty was signed, because news took weeks to cross the Atlantic.

questions.prompt: Which ancient Egyptian ruler ordered the construction at Abu Simbel?
questions.fact: The whole temple was cut apart and moved uphill in the 1960s to save it from a rising reservoir.

questions.prompt: The Bay of Pigs invasion targeted which country?
questions.fact: Its failure hardened the alliance it was meant to break, and led directly to the missile crisis a year later.

questions.prompt: Which people built the moai statues of Easter Island?
questions.fact: Many statues have full buried bodies below the famous heads, only revealed by excavation.

questions.prompt: Who was the first Holy Roman Emperor?
questions.fact: He reportedly could not write fluently, keeping a writing tablet under his pillow to practise at night.

questions.prompt: The Berlin Airlift supplied which city during a Soviet blockade?
questions.fact: At its peak an aircraft landed roughly every thirty seconds, sustaining two million people for almost a year.

questions.prompt: Which Roman structure could be flooded to stage mock naval battles?
questions.fact: The capability was lost once a network of underground chambers was built beneath the arena floor.

questions.prompt: Which country's civil war ended in 1939 with Franco in power?
questions.fact: It served as a testing ground for weapons and tactics both Germany and the Soviet Union used soon after.

questions.prompt: Which US movement was led in part by Susan B. Anthony?
questions.fact: She was arrested for voting in 1872, fined a hundred dollars, and refused to pay a cent of it.

questions.prompt: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 is notable for what?
options: Its length of under an hour
questions.fact: It is generally recorded as the shortest war in history, lasting roughly 38 minutes.

questions.prompt: Which pharaoh is associated with a brief shift to worshipping a single sun disc?
questions.fact: His successors tried to erase him from the records, which is partly why his son's tomb went unnoticed for so long.

questions.prompt: Which country did Napoleon invade in 1812 with disastrous results?
questions.fact: He entered with around 600,000 men and left with a fraction of that, most lost to cold, hunger and disease.

questions.prompt: The Underground Railroad helped people escape from what?
questions.fact: It was neither underground nor a railroad, but the railway vocabulary of stations and conductors served as code.

questions.prompt: Which Italian city-state was ruled by the Medici family?
questions.fact: They began as bankers, and their funding of artists is much of why the Renaissance happened where it did.

questions.prompt: Which US state was an independent republic before joining the Union?
questions.fact: It ran its own navy and diplomatic missions for nearly a decade before annexation.

questions.prompt: Which plague-carrying pandemic reached Europe in 1347 by ship?
questions.fact: Quarantine gets its name from the forty days Venetian ships were held offshore during outbreaks.

questions.prompt: Which African kingdom was known for its bronze plaques taken by British forces in 1897?
questions.fact: The plaques are held in museums across Europe and North America, and repatriation has been under way since 2021.

questions.prompt: Which conference in 1919 produced the post-war settlement of Europe?
questions.fact: An economist attending resigned in protest and wrote a book predicting the settlement would cause another war.

questions.prompt: Who commanded the Allied invasion of Normandy in 1944?
questions.fact: He wrote a note accepting full blame in case it failed, kept it in his wallet, and found it weeks later.

questions.prompt: Which ancient Greek was tutor to Alexander the Great?
questions.fact: Alexander reportedly carried an annotated copy of the Iliad from his tutor throughout his campaigns.

questions.prompt: The Gold Rush of 1849 drew prospectors to which US state?
questions.fact: Most miners lost money. The reliable fortunes were made selling them tools, food and trousers.

questions.prompt: Which empire was ended by the fall of Constantinople in 1453?
questions.fact: Scholars fleeing westward carried Greek manuscripts with them, feeding the Italian Renaissance directly.

questions.prompt: Which country did Britain hand back to China in 1997?
questions.fact: The handover happened because a 99-year lease on the surrounding territories expired, not the island itself.

questions.prompt: Which ship carried Charles Darwin on his survey voyage?
questions.fact: He was invited largely as a dinner companion for the captain, whose rank forbade socialising with the crew.

questions.prompt: The Hagia Sophia was built as what kind of building?
questions.fact: It held the record for the world's largest interior space for nearly a thousand years.

questions.prompt: Which country was ruled by apartheid until the early 1990s?
questions.fact: The system was formalised in 1948 and dismantled through negotiations that took four years to complete.

questions.prompt: The Domesday Book was commissioned by which king?
questions.fact: Its purpose was almost entirely fiscal: he wanted to know exactly what the country could be taxed.

questions.prompt: Which ancient city's walls are described in the Epic of Gilgamesh?
questions.fact: The poem opens and closes by praising the walls, framing the whole story as a monument the king left behind.

questions.prompt: Which country did the Soviet Union invade in 1956 to crush an uprising?
questions.fact: Around 200,000 people fled the country in the weeks that followed, most crossing on foot into Austria.

questions.prompt: Which trading company effectively governed large parts of India?
questions.fact: It maintained an army roughly twice the size of the British Army before the Crown took direct control in 1858.

questions.prompt: Which element makes up about 65 percent of the human body by mass?
questions.fact: Almost all of it is locked up in water rather than the air in your lungs.

questions.prompt: What is the name for the point at which a liquid becomes a gas?
questions.fact: It falls with altitude, which is why cooking instructions differ at high elevation and water boils cooler on Everest.

questions.prompt: What does an ecologist study?
questions.fact: The word ecosystem was coined only in 1935, long after the study itself began.

questions.prompt: Which type of blood vessel is thinnest?
questions.fact: Their walls are one cell thick, which is the whole point: gases have to pass straight through.

questions.prompt: What is the term for animals that maintain a stable internal temperature?
questions.fact: It costs enormously more food, which is why a lizard can live on a fraction of what a similar-sized mammal needs.

questions.prompt: Which scientist proposed the theory of continental drift?
questions.fact: He was ridiculed for decades because he could not explain what moved the continents. Seafloor spreading later supplied the answer.

questions.prompt: What is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust?
questions.fact: It was once more valuable than gold, because separating it from ore was so difficult before electricity.

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain regulates breathing and heart rate?
questions.fact: It runs these functions without conscious input, which is why you cannot hold your breath until you pass out and stay out.

questions.prompt: What is the study of insects called?
questions.fact: It is regularly confused with etymology, the study of word origins, which is itself a nice piece of etymology.

questions.prompt: Which gas makes up the majority of the air we exhale?
questions.fact: Nitrogen passes through untouched, and exhaled air still contains about 16 percent oxygen, which is what makes rescue breathing work.

questions.prompt: What is the term for a change in a DNA sequence?
questions.fact: Most have no effect at all, since much of the genome does not code for anything.

questions.prompt: Which force keeps a satellite in orbit?
questions.fact: An orbiting satellite is falling continuously, just moving sideways fast enough to keep missing the planet.

questions.prompt: What is the pH range of an acidic solution?
questions.fact: The scale is logarithmic, so a pH of 3 is a hundred times more acidic than a pH of 5.

questions.prompt: Which structure connects muscle to bone?
questions.fact: The Achilles is the thickest in the body and can withstand several times an adult's body weight in load.

questions.prompt: What is the closest planet to Earth on average over time?
questions.fact: Venus comes closest at its nearest approach, but Mercury spends more of its orbit near us than any other planet.

questions.prompt: Which vitamin deficiency causes rickets?
questions.fact: It surged in industrial cities where smog blocked the sunlight children needed to make it.

questions.prompt: What is the term for the splitting of an atomic nucleus?
questions.fact: It was discovered by accident in 1938, and the physicist who explained it was excluded from the Nobel that followed.

questions.prompt: Which organ is primarily affected by cirrhosis?
questions.fact: Scarring replaces working tissue, which is the one kind of liver damage the organ cannot regenerate its way out of.

questions.prompt: Which type of wave does sound travel as?
questions.fact: It cannot travel through a vacuum at all, which is why space is genuinely silent.

questions.prompt: What is the largest artery in the human body?
questions.fact: It is about the diameter of a garden hose, and every drop of blood leaving the heart's left side passes through it.

questions.prompt: Which process do bacteria use to reproduce?
questions.fact: Under ideal conditions some divide every twenty minutes, which is why food spoils so suddenly rather than gradually.

questions.prompt: What does a catalyst do to the activation energy of a reaction?
questions.fact: It provides an easier route rather than pushing harder, which is why it can be recovered unchanged afterwards.

questions.prompt: What is the scientific name for the windpipe?
questions.fact: It is held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage, with the gap at the back so the food pipe behind it can expand.

questions.prompt: Which particle is exchanged to produce the electromagnetic force?
questions.fact: It has no mass, which is why the force it carries reaches across the entire universe rather than fading out.

questions.prompt: Which layer of skin is the outermost?
questions.fact: Its outer cells are already dead, and you shed roughly 500 million of them every day.

questions.prompt: What is the unit of frequency?
questions.fact: Human hearing tops out around 20,000 of them, and that ceiling drops steadily with age.

questions.prompt: Which mineral is measured as 10 on the Mohs scale?
questions.fact: The scale is ordinal, not proportional: the gap between 9 and 10 is far larger than between 1 and 9.

questions.prompt: What is the term for a solution that resists changes in pH?
questions.fact: Blood is one, and it holds pH within a range so narrow that a shift of a few tenths is life threatening.

questions.prompt: Which type of galaxy is the Milky Way?
questions.fact: We only worked this out indirectly, since we cannot get outside it to look.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of red blood cells?
questions.fact: A single one makes the full circuit of the body roughly every minute.

questions.prompt: What is the process by which a solid becomes a gas directly?
questions.fact: Dry ice does it at ordinary pressure, which is why it produces fog rather than a puddle.

questions.prompt: Which human organ system includes the skin, hair and nails?
questions.fact: Skin is the body's largest organ, weighing more than the brain and liver combined.

questions.prompt: Which planet takes the longest to orbit the Sun?
questions.fact: It completed its first full orbit since discovery only in 2011, 165 years after being found.

questions.prompt: What is a group of cells working together to perform a function called?
questions.fact: There are four basic types in the human body, and everything from a heart to an eyelid is built from combinations of them.

questions.prompt: Which scale measures the intensity of tornadoes?
questions.fact: It rates the damage rather than the wind, because instruments rarely survive close enough to measure directly.

questions.prompt: What is the chemical formula for methane?
questions.fact: As a greenhouse gas it traps far more heat than carbon dioxide, but breaks down in the atmosphere much faster.

questions.prompt: Which blood type is the universal plasma donor?
questions.fact: It is the reverse of red cells: AB gives plasma to anyone, while O can receive plasma from anyone.

questions.prompt: What is the term for a star that suddenly increases dramatically in brightness?
questions.fact: The name means new, because early astronomers assumed a star had appeared where none had been.

questions.prompt: Which sense do bats primarily use to navigate in darkness?
questions.fact: They emit calls loud enough to deafen themselves, and briefly disconnect their own ear bones with each shout.

questions.prompt: What is the term for water containing dissolved salts from rock?
questions.fact: The dissolved minerals are why kettles fur up, and why soap lathers poorly in some regions.

questions.prompt: Which planet has the largest volcano in the solar system?
questions.fact: Olympus Mons is roughly the size of France and so wide that from its slopes the summit would sit below the horizon.

questions.prompt: What is the study of heredity called?
questions.fact: Its foundations came from a monk counting pea plants, work that went almost unread for thirty-five years.

questions.prompt: Which type of energy does a moving object possess?
questions.fact: It rises with the square of speed, which is why stopping distances grow so sharply as a car goes faster.

questions.prompt: Which organ produces bile?
questions.fact: The gallbladder only stores it, which is why removing that organ changes little about digestion.

questions.prompt: What is the name for an atom with a different number of neutrons?
questions.fact: Carbon dating works by measuring how much of one unstable version remains in organic material.

questions.prompt: Which colour of visible light has the longest wavelength?
questions.fact: It scatters least in air, which is why sunsets redden and why it is used for distant warning lights.

questions.prompt: What is the term for the outermost layer of the Earth?
questions.fact: Under the oceans it is only about six kilometres thick, thinner relative to the planet than an apple skin.

questions.prompt: Which body system is responsible for producing antibodies?
questions.fact: It keeps a memory of past infections, which is the entire principle vaccines exploit.

questions.prompt: Which physical quantity is measured in pascals?
questions.fact: Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 101,000 of them, which is roughly a kilogram pressing on every square centimetre of you.

questions.prompt: What is the largest type of white blood cell?
questions.fact: They mature into cells that engulf debris and pathogens whole, a process named for the Greek for devouring.

questions.prompt: Which theory describes the origin of the universe from a hot dense state?
questions.fact: The name was coined dismissively by an opponent of the idea, and stuck.

questions.prompt: Which structure in plants absorbs water and nutrients from soil?
questions.fact: Most of the absorbing is done by microscopic hairs, and many plants effectively outsource the job to fungi.

questions.prompt: What is the term for the amount of matter in an object?
questions.fact: It does not change with location, which is why an astronaut has the same amount on the Moon and weighs a sixth as much.

questions.prompt: Which chemical element is essential to haemoglobin?
questions.fact: Some marine animals use copper instead, which is why a horseshoe crab's blood is blue.

questions.prompt: Which unit expresses the amount of substance in chemistry?
questions.fact: One contains about 6.02 times ten to the twenty-third particles, a number chosen so atomic mass in grams comes out neat.

questions.prompt: Which part of a comet points away from the Sun?
questions.fact: It is pushed by solar wind rather than trailing behind, so on the outbound leg it precedes the comet.

questions.prompt: What is the term for a self-sustaining nuclear reaction?
questions.fact: The first controlled one was achieved under a disused squash court at the University of Chicago in 1942.

questions.prompt: Which class of animal are dolphins?
questions.fact: They sleep with one half of the brain at a time, because breathing for them is a conscious act.

questions.prompt: What is the SI unit of electric current?
questions.fact: It is defined by the force between two current-carrying wires, one of the few units tied to a physical effect rather than an object.

questions.prompt: Which process describes water moving from soil into the atmosphere via plants?
questions.fact: The Amazon moves so much water this way that it effectively creates its own rainfall.

questions.prompt: Which subatomic particles make up a proton?
questions.fact: Their combined mass accounts for only a small fraction of the proton's. The rest is the energy binding them.

questions.prompt: In boxing, what does TKO stand for?
questions.fact: It exists so a referee can stop a fight before a fighter is actually knocked unconscious.

questions.prompt: Which sport uses a sport-specific term called a bogey?
questions.fact: It comes from a Victorian song about a bogeyman, adopted by golfers as the phantom opponent they were chasing.

questions.prompt: How many players are on an Australian rules football team on the field?
questions.fact: The oval ground it is played on is borrowed from cricket, since the sport was invented to keep cricketers fit in winter.

questions.prompt: Which country dominates the sport of table tennis at Olympic level?
questions.fact: Its national trials are widely considered harder to win than the Olympics themselves.

questions.prompt: What is the term for scoring three goals in one ice hockey game?
questions.fact: Fans traditionally throw hats onto the ice, and the arena staff collect them during the next stoppage.

questions.prompt: Which race is known as the Greatest Show on Turf in horse racing's British calendar?
questions.fact: Its fences are named rather than numbered, and Becher's Brook is called after a rider who fell into it in 1839.

questions.prompt: How many points does a converted try earn in total in rugby union?
questions.fact: The conversion is kicked from a line drawn straight back from where the try was scored, so scoring nearer the posts helps.

questions.prompt: Which sport features a move called the Fosbury Flop?
questions.fact: It only became possible once landing pits changed from sand and sawdust to deep foam.

questions.prompt: In which sport do teams compete for the Webb Ellis Cup?
questions.fact: It is named after the schoolboy of the founding legend, a story historians consider almost certainly invented.

questions.prompt: How wide is a regulation football goal?
questions.fact: The figure is 8 yards converted, which is why it comes out at such an awkward metric number.

questions.prompt: Which sport is played with a puck and a curved stick on grass?
questions.fact: It is played with a ball rather than a puck, which is the detail this question is designed to catch.

questions.prompt: Which Olympic event involves shooting and fencing among five disciplines?
questions.fact: It was invented to simulate the skills of a 19th-century cavalry officer trapped behind enemy lines.

questions.prompt: In cricket, what is the fielding position directly behind the batter called?
questions.fact: They typically take more catches than any other fielder, and are the only player permitted gloves and pads.

questions.prompt: Which nation invented the sport of curling?
questions.fact: Every competition stone is quarried from a single small Scottish island, prized for granite that resists cracking.

questions.prompt: What is the diameter of a basketball hoop?
questions.fact: That is a little under twice the diameter of the ball, so a clean centred shot has surprisingly little margin.

questions.prompt: Which sport awards the Claret Jug?
questions.fact: The winner keeps a replica. The original goes back before the next championship, engraved with their name.

questions.prompt: Which country won the first Cricket World Cup in 1975?
questions.fact: They won the next one too, and the final in 1975 finished close to nine in the evening in midsummer London.

questions.prompt: Which sport features the terms jib, tack and spinnaker?
questions.fact: A boat cannot sail directly into the wind, so tacking is a zigzag that makes upwind progress at an angle.

questions.prompt: How long is a standard Olympic-distance triathlon run?
questions.fact: It follows a 1.5 kilometre swim and a 40 kilometre bike leg, and the run is where most races are decided.

questions.prompt: Which martial art is the national sport of Korea?
questions.fact: It became a full Olympic medal sport in 2000, after two Games as a demonstration event.

questions.prompt: In athletics, what is the standard height of a men's 110 metre hurdle?
questions.fact: The hurdles are weighted to tip forward if struck, a change made after athletes broke bones on rigid barriers.

questions.prompt: Which sport uses a term called a maiden over?
questions.fact: It means six balls bowled with no runs conceded, and the term dates back to at least the 1830s.

questions.prompt: Which country has won the most Tour de France titles by nationality?
questions.fact: No French rider has won it since 1985, which has become a running national frustration.

questions.prompt: Which sport is contested at the Crucible Theatre in Sheffield?
questions.fact: The venue seats under a thousand, making it far smaller than most sports would accept for a world final.

questions.prompt: How many minutes long is each quarter in an NBA game?
questions.fact: International basketball uses ten-minute quarters, which is why NBA and Olympic statistics do not compare directly.

questions.prompt: Which event is the shortest sprint on the Olympic athletics programme?
questions.fact: The 60 metres is contested indoors only, so the 100 is the shortest at a summer Games.

questions.prompt: Which sport features a position called the hooker?
questions.fact: The name describes the job: hooking the ball backwards with the foot once the scrum engages.

questions.prompt: Which sport uses the term birdie for one under par?
questions.fact: Badminton uses birdie too, but for the shuttlecock itself, which is where the confusion comes from.

questions.prompt: In which sport would you perform a triple axel?
questions.fact: It is the only jump taken off facing forwards, which adds an extra half rotation compared with every other triple.

questions.prompt: Which competition is contested by women's golfers of Europe and the United States?
questions.fact: It began in 1990, more than sixty years after the men's equivalent.

questions.prompt: How many pins are set at the start of a tenpin bowling frame?
questions.fact: The game exists because an earlier nine-pin version was banned in parts of America over gambling.

questions.prompt: Which position in football is the only one permitted to handle the ball?
questions.fact: Even then only inside the penalty area, a restriction introduced in 1912 after keepers began roaming.

questions.prompt: Which sport is played at Lord's, Headingley and Edgbaston?
questions.fact: All three are English Test grounds, and each has a distinct reputation for how the pitch behaves.

questions.prompt: Which Olympic sport involves a horse performing set movements to music?
questions.fact: The freestyle routine is judged partly on how well the horse's gait matches the chosen music.

questions.prompt: How many attempts does a shot putter get in an Olympic final?
questions.fact: The field is usually cut after three, with only the leaders taking the final three throws.

questions.prompt: Which country has hosted the Summer Olympics most often?
questions.fact: It has hosted four times and will host a fifth in 2028, more than any other nation.

questions.prompt: Which sport features an event called the omnium?
questions.fact: It combines four separate races into one score, making it cycling's closest equivalent to a decathlon.

questions.prompt: In baseball, what is a home run with the bases loaded called?
questions.fact: The term was borrowed from bridge, where it means winning every trick.

questions.prompt: Which sport uses a device called a starting block?
questions.fact: Both fit them with sensors, and a reaction under a tenth of a second is ruled a false start as physically impossible.

questions.prompt: Which team sport is played on ice with a broom?
questions.fact: Sweepers can extend a stone's travel by several metres, which makes them as important as the thrower.

questions.prompt: Which country won the men's football World Cup in 1966?
questions.fact: The trophy had been stolen months earlier and was found by a dog named Pickles under a hedge in south London.

questions.prompt: Which sport has a scoring zone called the D?
questions.fact: A goal only counts if the shot is taken inside it, which is why attacks funnel into a narrow area.

questions.prompt: How long does a standard boxing round last?
questions.fact: Women's professional rounds are usually two minutes, a difference that remains a live argument in the sport.

questions.prompt: Which sport features the Iron Man and Iron Woman events?
questions.fact: It combines swimming, board paddling, ski paddling and running, and is a major spectator sport in Australia.

questions.prompt: Which country's team is nicknamed the All Blacks?
questions.fact: The name may have come from a printer's error, with all backs misread as all blacks in a match report.

questions.prompt: In tennis, what score follows deuce for the serving player?
questions.fact: The word comes from the French for two-of, meaning two more points are needed to take the game.

questions.prompt: How heavy is a men's Olympic shot?
questions.fact: That is exactly sixteen pounds, another metric figure that gives itself away as an imperial conversion.

questions.prompt: Which sport features a race called the Paris-Roubaix?
questions.fact: Much of it runs over cobbles so rough that riders use wider tyres and extra padding on the handlebars.

questions.prompt: Which stadium is known as the Theatre of Dreams?
questions.fact: The nickname came from a former player turned commentator, and the club adopted it in its own marketing.

questions.prompt: How many events make up the women's heptathlon?
questions.fact: It replaced the pentathlon in 1984, and the 800 metres that closes it is regularly where the medals change hands.

questions.prompt: Which sport uses a term called love-forty?
questions.fact: It means the server has lost three straight points, and faces three chances for the opponent to take the game.

questions.prompt: Which country invented the sport of lacrosse?
questions.fact: It descends from games played by Indigenous nations, some involving hundreds of players and lasting days.

questions.prompt: Which Formula One team has won the most constructors' championships?
questions.fact: It is the only team to have competed in every season since the championship began in 1950.

questions.prompt: How many laps is the Indianapolis 500?
questions.fact: The winner traditionally drinks milk, a custom that began when a driver asked for buttermilk in 1936.

questions.prompt: Which sport features a technique called the butterfly?
questions.fact: It developed out of breaststroke, when swimmers realised the rules did not forbid recovering the arms over the water.

questions.prompt: Which trophy is awarded to the winner of the Premier League?
questions.fact: A second identical trophy exists so presentations can be staged simultaneously if the title is undecided on the final day.

questions.prompt: Which country has won the most Olympic gold medals in gymnastics?
questions.fact: Their dominance was built on a state system that identified and trained gymnasts from early childhood.

questions.prompt: Which sport is played at Roland Garros?
questions.fact: The venue is named after a First World War aviator, not a tennis player.

questions.prompt: How many minutes is a period of extra time in knockout football?
questions.fact: Two such periods are played in full, with no sudden death, after the golden goal experiment was abandoned in 2004.

questions.prompt: Which sport features the terms peloton and domestique?
questions.fact: Riding in the pack saves up to forty percent of a rider's energy, which is why breakaways so often fail.

questions.prompt: Which country hosted the 2016 Summer Olympics?

questions.prompt: Which company created the first mass-market personal computer spreadsheet-driven success, the Apple II?
questions.fact: It stayed in production for sixteen years, longer than almost any computer since.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym DNS resolve?
questions.fact: There are thirteen root server addresses worldwide, though each is actually many machines answering to the same address.

questions.prompt: Which programming language was designed by Bjarne Stroustrup?
questions.fact: The name is a programmer's joke: the ++ operator means add one to what came before.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of RAID in storage?
questions.fact: Some configurations survive a drive failing entirely, which is why it is standard in servers but rare in laptops.

questions.prompt: Which protocol secures web traffic with encryption?
questions.fact: It replaced SSL, though almost everyone still calls certificates SSL certificates out of habit.

questions.prompt: What is the name for a network attack that overwhelms a server with traffic?
questions.fact: Distributed versions use thousands of compromised machines, which is what makes them so hard to block by address.

questions.prompt: Which company created the PostScript page description language?
questions.fact: Combined with the laser printer and a Mac, it created desktop publishing more or less overnight.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym CPU cache reduce?
questions.fact: Fetching from main memory can cost the processor hundreds of idle cycles, which the cache exists to avoid.

questions.prompt: Which language is primarily used for styling and structuring data exchange as tags?
questions.fact: JSON largely displaced it for web APIs, being far less verbose for the same information.

questions.prompt: What is the term for testing software by feeding it random input?
questions.fact: It has found serious flaws in software that had passed years of careful hand-written tests.

questions.prompt: Which unit describes how many times a screen updates per second?
questions.fact: Cinema runs at 24 per second, which is why film looks different from video even on the same screen.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym VPN's tunnel do?
questions.fact: The outer connection hides what the inner one is doing, which is why it works on restricted networks.

questions.prompt: What is a repository in version control?
options: A store of code and its history
questions.fact: Git stores every version as a full snapshot rather than a set of differences, which is why history is so fast to search.

questions.prompt: Which company manufactures the M-series chips used in Macs?
questions.fact: They put processor and memory on the same package, which is much of why they run so cool for their speed.

questions.prompt: Which sorting algorithm has an average complexity of n log n and is widely used?
questions.fact: Its worst case is far slower, which is why real implementations shuffle or pick pivots carefully.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a CDN?
options: Serving content from servers near the user
questions.fact: Distance is a hard physical limit: light in fibre crosses the Atlantic in roughly thirty milliseconds at best.

questions.prompt: Which company created the Java programming language's current steward Oracle acquired?
questions.fact: The acquisition led to a decade-long lawsuit with Google over whether an API can be copyrighted.

questions.prompt: Which technology uses a distributed ledger with no central authority?
questions.fact: Its energy cost comes not from storing data but from making it expensive to rewrite history.

questions.prompt: What is the term for code that runs in a browser rather than on a server?
questions.fact: It can never be trusted for security, since the user controls the machine running it.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym API rate limiting prevent?
questions.fact: Well-designed limits return a header telling you when to try again, rather than simply refusing.

questions.prompt: Which storage medium held about 700 megabytes?
questions.fact: Its 74-minute capacity is often said to have been chosen so Beethoven's Ninth would fit on one disc.

questions.prompt: What is the name for software that holds data hostage until payment?
questions.fact: Attacks increasingly target backups first, since a working backup removes any reason to pay.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym GPS's rival GLONASS belong to?
questions.fact: Most modern phones use several systems at once, which is why fixes are faster than they were a decade ago.

questions.prompt: Which term describes making software work in another language and region?
questions.fact: The hardest parts are usually dates, plurals and text direction rather than the words themselves.

questions.prompt: What is the function of a database index?
questions.fact: Each one speeds reads and slows writes, so adding them everywhere makes a database worse rather than better.

questions.prompt: Which company created the Linux distribution Red Hat Enterprise Linux?
questions.fact: It sells support rather than software, a model that made a large business out of something given away free.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym HTTP status 404 indicate?
questions.fact: The 4 at the start means the client's request was at fault, which is why 500 codes blame the server instead.

questions.prompt: Which technology allows a single machine to run multiple isolated operating systems?
questions.fact: Containers do something similar with far less overhead by sharing one kernel rather than emulating hardware.

questions.prompt: What is the term for the first version of a product released for testing?
questions.fact: Beta follows it, and the practice of public betas began largely because testing at scale is impossible in-house.

questions.prompt: Which company created the Firefox browser?
questions.fact: It grew out of Netscape's code being released as open source after the company lost the browser war.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym SEO stand for?
questions.fact: Search engines deliberately keep ranking details secret, because publishing them would make gaming trivial.

questions.prompt: Which measure describes the delay before data starts arriving?
questions.fact: It is why satellite internet feels sluggish even at high speeds: the signal has to travel to orbit and back.

questions.prompt: Which company developed the ARM architecture originally?
questions.fact: It was designed by a tiny team for a British home computer, and now ships in tens of billions of devices.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a hash function in security?
questions.fact: It is deliberately one-way, which is why a stolen password database is not the same as stolen passwords.

questions.prompt: Which format is commonly used for lossy audio compression?
questions.fact: It discards sound the ear is unlikely to notice, a technique borrowed from research into human hearing.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym UI stand for?
questions.fact: UX is the broader experience, so a beautiful interface can still sit inside a terrible one.

questions.prompt: Which company created the Kubernetes container system?
questions.fact: It grew out of an internal system used to run Google's own services for over a decade.

questions.prompt: What is the term for a copy of a website stored to serve faster?
questions.fact: Deciding when to discard it is famously one of the two hardest problems in computing, alongside naming things.

questions.prompt: Which company introduced the first commercially available laser printer?
questions.fact: Xerox invented the technology but IBM shipped a product first, an early example of a pattern that repeated for them.

questions.prompt: Which term describes writing tests before the code they test?
questions.fact: The discipline is as much about designing the interface first as about catching bugs.

questions.prompt: Which company created the Photoshop-rival GIMP?
questions.fact: It began as a university project in 1995 and has been maintained by contributors ever since.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym LED's successor OLED add?
questions.fact: Because each pixel makes its own light, switching one off produces genuine black rather than dark grey.

questions.prompt: Which company owns the WhatsApp messaging service?
questions.fact: It was bought for around nineteen billion dollars when it had roughly fifty employees.

questions.prompt: What is the term for combining code changes from different branches?
questions.fact: Conflicts arise only when two branches change the same lines, which is why small frequent changes hurt less.

questions.prompt: Which wireless generation introduced widespread mobile video streaming?
questions.fact: 3G made it technically possible; 4G made it cheap enough that people actually did it.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym CMS stand for in web publishing?
questions.fact: WordPress alone powers a substantial share of all websites, which makes its security everyone's problem.

questions.prompt: Which term describes reducing an image's file size by discarding detail?
questions.fact: Repeatedly saving the same file this way degrades it each time, which is where visibly mangled memes come from.

questions.prompt: Which company created the Nintendo Switch?
questions.fact: It followed the company's worst-selling home console, and became one of the best-selling of all time.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym SQL injection exploit?
questions.fact: It has been in published top-ten vulnerability lists for over twenty years and still appears regularly.

questions.prompt: Which term describes a single point of failure being eliminated?
questions.fact: Achieving it properly means duplicating the thing you forgot about, which is usually the power or the network.

questions.prompt: Which company created the Raspberry Pi?
questions.fact: It was designed to get children programming again, and sold to industry in far greater numbers than expected.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym MFA describe?
questions.fact: A hardware key is the strongest common form, because it verifies the site as well as the user.

questions.prompt: Which language is used to query relational databases?
questions.fact: Every database vendor has its own dialect, so queries rarely move between systems unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which company created the Tor anonymity network's original design?
questions.fact: It only provides anonymity if many different people use it, so its designers needed it to be public.

questions.prompt: Which technology powers most electric vehicle batteries today?
questions.fact: The chemistry won a Nobel Prize in 2019, roughly thirty years after it first reached consumers in camcorders.

questions.prompt: Which company created the Slack messaging platform?
questions.fact: It was the internal chat tool built for a game that flopped, and the tool outlived the game.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a firewall rule?
options: To permit or block specific traffic
questions.fact: Default-deny is the safer design: block everything, then allow only what is needed.

questions.prompt: Which company developed the first widely adopted smartphone touchscreen keyboard?
questions.fact: Its predictive correction was what made a glass keyboard usable, and it was considered the riskiest part of the design.
